newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. insists on permanent seats for Germany, Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insists on permanent seats for Germany, Japan.

text.p: The United States, which has long supported giving Germany and Japan permanent seats on the Security Council, said on Wednesday it could not agree to any expansion of the council unless that happened.
"Japan and Germany would both be valuable new permanent members whose contributions would strengthen the council," ambassador Edward Gnehm of the United States told the General Assembly.
"And, indeed, the U.S. could not agree to a council enlargement that did not entail their permanent membership," he added.

The Assembly was debating the latest report of a U.N. working group on council reform which has reached consensus on an unspecified increase in the size of the 15-nation body but, after nearly three years, has still not agreed how this should be done.

The council currently consists of five veto-bearing permanent members who were the main victors in the Second World War -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- and 10 non-permanent members who serve two-year terms.
Among unresolved issues are whether any new permanent seats should be added, and if so, whether they should also carry the power of veto.

Gnehm said the United States would accept a "modest expansion of the council beyond permanent seats for Germany and Japan," while keeping firmly in mind the need to maintain the council's working efficiency.

"Beyond Germany and Japan, additional membership remains a substantial question. While we take no position on how other seats might be apportioned, we believe the total size of the council should not exceed about 20 seats," he said.

The United States also opposed any change in the status, powers and obligations of the current permanent members, all of which were "countries with global political and economic influence and a capacity to contribute to peace and security through concrete measures on a global basis," Gnehm added.
